entries.title: NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe and Granary v2: Intelligent Multilingual Transcription You Can Prompt and Adapt
entries.content:
nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe-30B-A4B

Automatic Speech Recognition • 34B • Updated • 338 • 166

NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe and Granary v2: Intelligent Multilingual Transcription You Can Prompt and Adapt

Enterprise + Article

One open model for multilingual transcription, speaker attribution, translation, and audio Q&A, with top leaderboard results, plus the open Granary v2 data pipeline and fine-tuning recipes to adapt it.

A transcript can capture every spoken word and still leave users or applications wondering who said what, how to translate it, or how to format domain-specific jargon. Multilingual calls, fast-paced meetings, and medical dictation each need different output: a translation, speaker labels, or correctly spelled medical terms.

NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe is an open-weight, promptable model that turns recorded speech into useful text, now available on Hugging Face and ModelScope. It brings transcription, speaker attribution (diarization), translation, and audio question answering into one checkpoint: it transcribes 40 languages, translates 31 of them to or from English, and attributes speakers in 13. It handles recordings up to an hour long and labels up to eight speakers. Developers can guide output with natural language, choose where their audio is processed, and adapt recognition to domain vocabulary and accents.

Transcribe is first among open-weight models on the Hugging Face Open ASR Leaderboard for English and sits on Artificial Analysis’s accuracy–active-parameter frontier. For speaker attribution, it posts the lowest error rate on David AI’s 21-language diarization leaderboard and ranks first in VoiceArena’s 14-system comparison. Quantized versions are coming soon, so you can run Transcribe locally on your RTX Spark, DGX Spark, or Jetson AGX Thor—or scale up on Blackwell data-center GPUs.

Granary v2’s multilingual data (available on Hugging Face and ModelScope) and reusable curation pipeline, together with NeMo Speech fine-tuning tools, extend prompt-level control to training: developers can define the written form they need and adapt the model to the speech their applications encounter. In a medical case study, fine-tuning cut word error rate (WER) on held-out speakers by 45.8% relative to the best prompt.

Guide transcription and analysis with natural language

The same checkpoint can turn one meeting recording into different outputs, depending on the instruction:

  • “Transcribe this recording and label each speaker.”
  • “Translate this audio into English.”
  • “What decisions were made in this meeting?”

Experience the model in action in the video below, where it tackles a classic scene from the 1940 screwball comedy His Girl Friday—a film famous for its rapid-fire, heavily overlapping dialogue.

Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe captions a scene from His Girl Friday (1940) and labels speakers, including overlapping dialogue.

For unfamiliar terms, try context before training. In a healthcare setting, for example:

Transcribe this medical discussion in the original language. Possible terms: HbA1c, metformin. Use these terms only when supported by the audio. Preserve standard medical spelling and write numbers in conventional written form.

The model card has recommended presets, including reasoning for audio questions, plus the full prompt guide and a task-by-language matrix: language support differs by task, and audio question answering is trained in English. Word-level timestamps are also supported. As with any speech model, spot-check names, speaker changes, and answers against the recording.

From live classes to lasting lessons. Agora, whose real-time voice and video platform powers live conversations in apps, used word-level timestamps in a classroom demo: Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe turns a recorded class into a transcript shown alongside the replay, so students can see what was said and when. Agora’s blog walks through how they built it.

Leaderboard wins from transcription to speaker attribution

Among open-weight models, Transcribe leads on what was said; on who said it, it tops two speaker-attribution benchmarks outright.

Hugging Face Open ASR Leaderboard. The leaderboard measures transcription accuracy as word error rate (WER) on public test sets, in three tracks:

  • English: first among open-weight models at 5.33% average WER (Figure 1).
  • Multilingual: 4.62% mean WER across seven languages, the lowest among evaluated open-weight models in the model card’s Open ASR comparison.
  • Long-form: 10.98% mean WER, also the lowest in that comparison.

Figure 1. Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe ranks first among open-weight models on the Hugging Face Open ASR Leaderboard (English) at 5.33% average WER, with API models excluded. Lower WER means fewer transcription errors.

Artificial Analysis Speech-to-Text Leaderboard. Artificial Analysis independently ranks speech-to-text models by AA-WER, its word error rate index. Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe ties for first among open-weight models at 2.8% AA-WER, with about 4B active parameters versus 24B for the model it ties. On AA-AgentTalk, the held-out voice-agent speech set that makes up 50% of the AA-WER index, Transcribe scores 1.8% WER, versus 2.3% for the next-best open-weight model. Transcribe pairs its speech encoder with a hybrid Mamba–Transformer mixture-of-experts language model, so only about 4B of its 30B parameters are active per token. That puts it on Artificial Analysis’s open-weight Pareto frontier of accuracy versus active parameters. On AA’s all-model chart, it ranks ahead of several widely used proprietary speech APIs.

Figure 2. Leading AA accuracy at about one-sixth the active parameters: Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe achieves 2.80% AA-WER with approximately 4B active parameters.

Speaker attribution across languages and overlap. Sortformer speaker cues reach the language model with the acoustic features, so Transcribe can tag each turn during generation instead of relying solely on a later step to attach speakers to words.

David AI DAI-ASR-I18N Leaderboard. On David AI’s DAI-ASR-I18N combined transcription-and-speaker-attribution track, Transcribe ranks first among evaluated open-weight models and second overall. On the benchmark’s diarization track, which scores who spoke when across 21 languages, it has the lowest diarization error rate of the 14 systems tested, slightly ahead of NVIDIA’s dedicated Nemotron 3 Diarization model.

Figure 3. NVIDIA models hold the top two spots on David AI’s multilingual diarization leaderboard: Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe posts the lowest overall diarization error rate (DER), 18.26% across 21 languages, followed by Nemotron 3 Diarization at 18.38%. DER measures speaker-time errors; lower is better.

VoiceArena Diarization-Bench. On VoiceArena’s English full-session benchmark, Transcribe posts the lowest concatenated minimum-permutation WER (cpWER) of 14 systems and ranks first in both in-person and online settings. It also drops the fewest words: deletions are 8.32% of reference words, versus a median of about 31%.

Figure 4. NVIDIA models hold the top two spots in VoiceArena’s 14-system comparison: Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe leads at 32.4% cpWER, followed by NVIDIA Multitalker Parakeet with Nemotron 3 Diarization at 34.2%. Diarization-Bench v1 covers English full sessions, overlapping speech and 2–8 speakers. cpWER counts word errors after matching speaker labels; lower is better.

More evaluations. Ocular AI’s Converse-STT evaluation ranks Transcribe the top open model. Josh Talks’ Voice of India leaderboard reports Transcribe’s results across Indian languages.

High-throughput transcription. In benchmarking, Transcribe processed 100 hours of audio in under three minutes on one NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPU, using the forthcoming NVFP4 quantized version. Results were measured on 30-second clips at high concurrency.

Serve the available checkpoint with vLLM today. Local deployment with NeMo-Speech.cpp is coming soon alongside the quantized versions. Transcribe is built for recorded audio, not live streaming.

Specialized recordings can still call for adaptation to domain vocabulary and transcript conventions. Granary v2 and NeMo Speech fine-tuning address that, starting with the data behind Transcribe.

Granary v2: The open data curation pipeline behind Transcribe

A promptable speech model requires training data with unambiguous formatting targets. Granary v2 is part of the Nemotron speech collection on Hugging Face and ModelScope. Built with NVIDIA NeMo Curator, its reusable pipeline prepared multilingual speech used in Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe’s training, producing aligned transcript variants, task labels, and inspectable quality metadata. The public manifest covers 463,062 hours across 48 languages and 16 source corpora, up from 25 languages in Granary v1. These figures describe the dataset release, not Transcribe’s full training mixture or its sampling weights.

Granary v2 generates three transcript forms for each recording (Table 1), the same verbatim and clean styles developers can request from Transcribe with a prompt. Beyond transcription, the pipeline produces short audio captions, code-switching restoration of loanwords, speech-grounded Q&A pairs, contextual ASR biasing terms, and translations with automatic quality scores.

Training targetIllustrative transcript
Text-normalized, verbatimI paid, uh, twenty-five euros.
Inverse text normalization, with disfluenciesI paid, uh, €25.
Inverse text normalization, without disfluenciesI paid €25.

Table 1. Granary v2 training targets for the same utterance.

The pipeline is organized into four reusable stages:

  • 1. Audio Preparation (Metadata): Segments raw or long-form audio, tracks speakers across the full recording, and tags acoustic events and language. Granary v2’s sources were already segmented, so this release skipped this stage.
  • 2. Transcription (ASR): Routes each language to primary and recovery ASR models, falling back when the primary fails a hallucination check. Human reference transcripts help preserve trusted spellings while adding spoken forms and disfluencies.
  • 3. Task Label Generation (Text): Derives transcript variants, then checks character rate, hallucination patterns, and model or human-reference agreement. Only accepted records receive contextual-ASR terms and translations.
  • 4. High Fidelity (HiFi): Filters out segments that are noisy, clipped, or contain multiple speakers, keeping a smaller set of high-quality recordings for uses beyond ASR. For the VoxPopuli dataset, it reduced 354k hours to 111k hours across 22 European languages.

Figure 6. Granary v2 data curation pipeline, following one sample from raw audio through the Metadata, ASR, and Text stages to a training example.

Developers can run the NeMo Curator pipeline with Ray and NVIDIA Dynamo backends on their own recordings or authorized public corpora, or build on the Granary v2 public manifests. The manifests include the three transcript forms as tn_raw, itn_raw, and itn_clean, the labels described above, entity hints, derived instruction pairs, provenance, and a per-record quality flag. Download source audio separately under each corpus’s original license, and follow the release’s published terms.

Adapt recognition to the vocabulary that matters

Start with a development-set prompt that specifies language, script, and transcript format. In the case study below, naming English and the Latin alphabet in the prompt cut full-benchmark WER from 30.8% to 23.8%. For domain errors that remain, the NeMo Speech fine-tuning workflow pairs representative speech with explicit written targets.

The NeMo Speech medical ASR case study shows this progression on Eka Care’s open benchmark of recordings from Indian doctors and medical students, which has 3,619 clips and no designated training split. The study builds adaptation data from generated medical text and public medicine catalogs, then combines approximately 153 hours of synthetic speech, 29 hours of accented English from Common Voice, and 63 hours of medical recordings from MultiMed.

Figure 7. On the full test set of Eka Care’s Indian medical speech benchmark, a better prompt cuts WER from 30.8% to 23.8%, and fine-tuning brings it to 11.8%, about 62% fewer transcription errors than the model out of the box. The full set includes the 855 tuning clips used to choose the prompt and checkpoints; the held-out results below are the cleaner test.

Synthetic generation separates the written target from its spoken rendering: “HbA1c” is the label, while “H B A one C” is sent to the synthesizer. Multiple TTS voices broaden the audio; real recordings add accents and recording conditions. Training text is filtered for exact matches and shared eight-word sequences with benchmark references.

As with Granary v2’s explicit targets, training examples vary digits, unit spacing, company-name expansion, and brand-name hyphens, with instructions specifying the required convention. Some prompts include term lists with near-miss distractors, so the model learns to use a spelling only when the audio supports it. The final system uses one fixed convention prompt and one model pass, without retrieval or transcript post-processing.

The recipe trains the speech encoder and projection and uses LoRA to adapt the language model. Two runs use different data mixtures; after adapter merging, selected checkpoints are uniformly averaged into one final model. Checkpoint selection uses decoded development-set results, rather than training loss alone. The full adaptation, from text generation through evaluation, took about 14 GPU-hours on one NVIDIA GB300.

Domain gains, measured on held-out speakers

The study splits the benchmark by speaker into 855 tuning clips, used to choose the prompt and checkpoints, and 2,764 held-out clips, decoded once per final system. Using Eka Care’s KARMA scoring pipeline, fine-tuning cuts held-out WER from 22.44% for the best-prompt baseline to 12.17%, a 45.8% relative reduction and the clearest evidence that the gains generalize to new speakers. Keyword WER falls from 9.2% to 6.5%, and semantic WER from 10.0% to 7.6%. On the same held-out speakers and scorer, the adapted model’s 12.17% WER beats an open medical-specialist model (13.79%) and a widely used general-purpose ASR model (14.92%).

On general English, LibriSpeech test-clean WER rises slightly, from 1.54% to 1.69%. The medical specialist still leads on exact matches for brand-name drugs and diagnostics; the study points to real recordings of clinicians saying brand names as the next step. For your own domain, keep at least 100 real, labeled clips for checkpoint selection, and evaluate the entity types your application depends on alongside general-speech retention.

The case study includes commands to reproduce each step. The fine-tuning tutorials cover recipes, resource requirements, and tools for training, export, and evaluation, including new-language and code-switching ASR. The accompanying agent skill lets a coding agent run the workflow, from baseline selection and data checks through training validation, adapter merging, and evaluation.

ModelScope also enables developers to fine-tune Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe through its ms-swift framework for specialized multimodal applications.

Get started with Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe and Granary v2

Try Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe in the Hugging Face demo or on ModelScope Studios, then download the checkpoint from Hugging Face or ModelScope. For self-hosted transcription, get started with vLLM or SGLang-Omni, both offering support from day one.

To skip self-hosting, use a hosted endpoint from Baseten, DeepInfra, or Simplismart.

To adapt it to your domain, start with the Granary v2 manifests on Hugging Face or ModelScope and the medical ASR case study, or let a coding agent drive the workflow with the fine-tuning agent skill.

entries.title: Build specialized multimodal models with LFM3
entries.content:
LiquidAI/LFM2.5-8B-A1B

Text Generation • 8B • Updated • 30.7k • 798

Build specialized multimodal models with LFM3

Team Article

LFM3 is our new generation of Liquid Foundation Models (LFMs), built to be the starting point for specialized intelligence. It brings text, vision, audio, omni, and decision models onto one shared backbone, all in the 2B parameter range. This means you can pick the model for your modality, fine-tune it on your own data on a single GPU, and deploy it where your application runs.

LFM3 brings four main changes compared to our previous LFM2 family:

  • More capability per parameter: a new tri-hybrid architecture and training recipe allow LFM3-1.7B to outperform LFM2.5-2.6B while using 35% fewer parameters.
  • Every modality on one backbone: six 2B-class models (text, vision, audio, omni, and decision) trained from LFM3-1.7B-Base, including our first omni model and video input for our vision model.
  • Built for the edge: the text model fits in about 1 GB at 4-bit precision, new in-house vision and audio encoders speed up processing, and the text model’s 256K context window lets agents run on-device.
  • Made to be specialized: every model fine-tunes on a single GPU, so you can adapt it to your data, terminology, and deployment environment.

How we built a more expressive backbone

LFM2 showed that a hybrid of short convolutions and attention can run fast on-device without sacrificing quality. For LFM3, we used our hardware-in-the-loop architecture search to redesign that architecture for agentic use cases, which need more capability per parameter and fast inference over long contexts. The search now covers 14 device and backend combinations, from phones and a Raspberry Pi 5 to laptops, cloud CPUs, GPUs, and the Qualcomm Hexagon NPU.

LFM3-1.7B-Base has 24 layers and four main changes:

  • Tri-hybrid layer mix: 13 gated short convolutions, 5 sliding-window attention (SWA) layers with a 256-token window, and 6 global attention layers. The convolutions use a kernel size of 7, up from 3 in LFM2.
  • Head-wise gated attention: a sigmoid gate scales each head's output, so a head can switch off when it has nothing to add. This can help suppress activation outliers that hurt quantization.
  • Partial RoPE: global attention layers rotate only the highest-frequency half of each head, so the other half matches on content regardless of distance. SWA layers keep full RoPE.
  • Sandwich norm: each block normalizes both its input and its output to keep activations well-scaled.

The payoff shows at long context. Per parameter, LFM3-1.7B matches LFM2-1.2B on short prompts across edge devices, and with 8K tokens in context it is about 25% faster. LFM3-1.7B-Base was pre-trained on 22T tokens with the same 128K vocabulary as LFM2.5-8B-A1B. The final 3.5T tokens are a mid-training stage on curated data with a larger share of agentic traces and tool calls, which also extends the context window to 256K tokens.

One backbone for six models

Every LFM3 model branches from LFM3-1.7B-Base. Instead of running one large general-purpose model, you pick the one that fits your inputs, customize it, and run it on-device.

ModelInputOutputBuilt on
LFM3-1.7B TextTextLFM3-1.7B-Base
LFM3-VL-2B Text, images, videoTextLFM3 backbone + vision encoder
LFM3-Audio-2B Text, audioText, speechLFM3 backbone + audio encoder, audio decoder, and LiquidCodec
LFM3-Omni-2B Text, images, video, audioText, speechLFM3 backbone + vision and audio encoders and audio decoder
d1-2B Text, images, videoCalibrated answersLFM3-VL-2B
d1-omni-2B Text, images, video, audioCalibrated answersLFM3-Omni-2B

The vision and audio models also get two new in-house encoders:

  • Vision encoder: it combines convolution and attention and uses 3x less compute than the SigLIP2 encoder in previous LFM VL models. Our 164M-parameter encoder matches Qwen3.5-2B's vision encoder in accuracy while requiring 2.2x fewer FLOPs (both measured with the same LFM2.5-230M language backbone). For video, it embeds each pair of sampled frames into one temporal slice, halving the temporal sequence length.
  • Audio encoder and LiquidCodec: the audio encoder mixes sliding-window attention and short convolutions and is fully causal, so the model can prefill while you speak, with time to first token as low as 50 ms. LiquidCodec, our new audio tokenizer, turns generated tokens into speech at about 87x real time on a single CPU thread on Apple M4 Max and supports streaming decoding.

How to use the LFM3 models

Each model runs in 

transformers
. The snippets below come from the model cards, which also list the other inference engines each model supports.

LFM3-1.7B

Reach for LFM3-1.7B when you need local agents, tool calling, structured outputs, or a base for domain-specific fine-tuning. It is post-trained to run in agentic harnesses such as Hermes Agent, Pi, and OpenClaw. It outperforms its predecessor, LFM2.5-2.6B, with 35% fewer parameters, and the biggest gains are on agentic tasks: on WebArena-Verified, it scores 38.42 against 3.02, and it even beats Qwen3.5-9B on long tasks in browsers and business apps. You can find more details in the LFM3-1.7B model card.

To run LFM3-1.7B, install the latest version of 

transformers
:
pip install -U transformers

Then load and run the model:

from transformers import pipeline

generator = pipeline(
    "text-generation",
    model="LiquidAI/LFM3-1.7B",
    trust_remote_code=True,
)

messages = [{"role": "user", "content": "What is C. elegans?"}]
output = generator(
    messages,
    do_sample=True,
    temperature=0.1,
    top_k=50,
    repetition_penalty=1.1,
    max_new_tokens=2048,
)
print(output[0]["generated_text"][-1]["content"])

For local agent setup, see the Agent Harnesses guide.

LFM3-VL-2B

Reach for LFM3-VL-2B when you need on-device visual understanding. It is the first LFM vision model that takes video as input; it reasons step by step before it answers, and it finds objects and reasons about how they are placed, a strong foundation for robotics. Compared with LFM2.5-VL-3B, it has fewer parameters (1.9B against 3.1B) yet raises the average across 62 vision benchmarks from 57.6 to 71.4, on par with Gemma 4 12B, a model more than six times larger. You can find more details in the LFM3-VL-2B model card.

To run LFM3-VL-2B, install transformers>=5.21.0 with its vision dependencies:

pip install "transformers>=5.21.0" torch torchvision pillow

Then load and run the model:

import torch
from transformers import AutoModelForImageTextToText, AutoProcessor

model_id = "LiquidAI/LFM3-VL-2B"

model = AutoModelForImageTextToText.from_pretrained(model_id, dtype=torch.bfloat16, device_map="auto", trust_remote_code=True)
processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id, trust_remote_code=True)

messages = [
    {
        "role": "user",
        "content": [
            {"type": "image", "url": "https://placecats.com/300/200"},
            {"type": "text", "text": "Describe this image."},
        ],
    }
]

inputs = processor.apply_chat_template(
    messages,
    add_generation_prompt=True,
    tokenize=True,
    return_dict=True,
    return_tensors="pt",
).to(model.device)

with torch.inference_mode():
    output_ids = model.generate(
        **inputs,
        do_sample=True,
        temperature=0.1,
        top_k=50,
        repetition_penalty=1.1,
        max_new_tokens=16384,  # generate() needs an explicit limit; reasoning can be long
    )

generated_ids = output_ids[:, inputs["input_ids"].shape[1] :]
print(processor.batch_decode(generated_ids, skip_special_tokens=True)[0])

See the LFM3-VL-2B model card for tool calling, tool search, and on-device inference with llama.cpp.

LFM3-Audio-2B

Reach for LFM3-Audio-2B when you need voice chat, speech recognition, speech synthesis, or translation across 18 languages on a laptop or edge device. It takes text or audio as input and responds with text, speech, or both, and it can turn spoken requests into tool calls. Compared with LFM2.5-Audio-1.5B, it uses a new in-house audio encoder and speech codec, speaks with higher quality (UTMOSv2 3.83 against 3.22), and adds audio understanding, general-purpose audio reasoning, and tool calling. You can find more details in the LFM3-Audio-2B model card.

To run LFM3-Audio-2B, install 

transformers>=5.20.2
with its audio dependencies:
pip install "transformers>=5.20.2" torch accelerate librosa soundfile

Load the model and processor directly from the Hugging Face Hub:

import torch
import soundfile as sf

from transformers import AutoModelForMultimodalLM, AutoProcessor

model_id = "LiquidAI/LFM3-Audio-2B"
device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"
dtype = torch.bfloat16 if device == "cuda" else torch.float32

model = AutoModelForMultimodalLM.from_pretrained(
    model_id, dtype=dtype, device_map=device, trust_remote_code=True
).eval()
processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id, trust_remote_code=True)
codec = processor.audio_tokenizer.to(device=device).eval()

Then ask a question aloud and get a reply in text and speech:

conversation = [
    {"role": "system", "content": "Respond with interleaved text and audio."},
    {"role": "user", "content": [{"type": "audio", "audio": "question.wav"}]},
    {"role": "assistant", "content": "<|mixed_start|>"},
]
inputs = processor.apply_chat_template(
    conversation,
    continue_final_message=True,
    tokenize=True,
    return_dict=True,
    return_tensors="pt",
).to(device)
with torch.no_grad():
    outputs = model.generate(
        **inputs,
        max_new_tokens=1024,
        audio_temperature=1.0,
        audio_top_k=128,
        audio_repetition_penalty=1.1,
        audio_repetition_window=4096,
        return_dict_in_generate=True,
    )

    text = processor.decode(
        outputs.sequences[0, inputs["input_ids"].shape[1]:],
        skip_special_tokens=True,
    )
    waveform = codec.decode(
        outputs.audio_codes[:1, :, :outputs.audio_lengths[0]]
    ).audio_values[0]  # 24 kHz
print(text)
sf.write("reply.wav", waveform.float().cpu().numpy(), 24_000)

See the LFM3-Audio-2B model card for live speech recognition, speech synthesis, audio understanding, and tool calling.

LFM3-Omni-2B

Reach for LFM3-Omni-2B when you need one on-device model that sees, listens, and talks back, in place of a separate ASR model, vision-language model, LLM, and TTS model. It can answer spoken questions about an image, watch and listen to a video together, and turn what it sees and hears into tool calls. It is our first omni model, with text, vision, and audio input and both text and speech output, and it keeps the core capabilities of the standalone LFM3 models, including visual question answering, speech recognition, speech synthesis, and instruction following. Like LFM3-Audio-2B, it speaks through LiquidCodec, which turns generated tokens into speech faster than real time, so spoken replies stream as the model generates them. On audio-visual video understanding, it beats models up to 10.7B parameters, such as Qwen2.5-Omni-7B, on Daily-Omni, WorldSense, and AV-SpeakerBench. You can find more details in the LFM3-Omni-2B model card.

To run LFM3-Omni-2B, install 

transformers>=5.20.2
with its vision and audio dependencies:
pip install "transformers>=5.20.2" torch torchvision torchcodec accelerate pillow librosa soundfile

import torch
import soundfile as sf

from transformers import AutoModelForMultimodalLM, AutoProcessor

model_id = "LiquidAI/LFM3-Omni-2B"
device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"
dtype = torch.bfloat16 if device == "cuda" else torch.float32

model = AutoModelForMultimodalLM.from_pretrained(
    model_id, dtype=dtype, device_map=device, trust_remote_code=True
).eval()
processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id, trust_remote_code=True)
codec = processor.audio_tokenizer.to(device=device).eval()

Then ask a question about a photo by voice:

conversation = [
    {
        "role": "system",
        "content": "Answer questions about the provided image. Base every answer only on what can be seen. Respond with text.",
    },
    {
        "role": "user",
        "content": [
            {"type": "image", "image": "photo.jpg"},
            {"type": "audio", "audio": "question.wav"},
        ],
    },
]
inputs = processor.apply_chat_template(
    conversation,
    add_generation_prompt=True,
    tokenize=True,
    return_dict=True,
    return_tensors="pt",
).to(device)

with torch.no_grad():
    outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=1024, generation_mode="text")

print(processor.decode(
    outputs.sequences[0, inputs["input_ids"].shape[1]:outputs.sequence_lengths[0]],
    skip_special_tokens=True,
))

See the LFM3-Omni-2B model card for speech output, video with its soundtrack, and tool calling.

d1-2B and d1-omni-2B

Reach for the d1 models when you need fast, structured decisions instead of generated text. Give them a situation (a support ticket, an invoice, an app screen, a photo, a voice note) and a list of questions, and they answer all of them in a single forward pass, each with a calibrated probability. Beyond yes/no, choices, and scores, they can now point at objects, read values from documents, estimate numbers with a range, and pick every option that applies. You can find more details in the model cards for d1-2B and d1-omni-2B.

Between the two d1 models:

  • d1-2B: choose it for text, pictures, and video. It replaces d1-3B with a third fewer parameters and scores higher on all four of our decision suites, for example, 75.5 against 64.0 on ImajevBench.
  • d1-omni-2B: choose it when your inputs include audio. If you ask by voice instead of in writing, it keeps nearly all of its accuracy.

To run d1-2B, install 

transformers>=5.19
with its vision dependencies:
pip install "transformers>=5.19" torch torchvision pillow

Then load d1-2B and ask it several questions about one support ticket in a single pass:

import torch
from transformers import AutoModel

device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "mps" if torch.backends.mps.is_available() else "cpu"
dtype = torch.float32 if device == "cpu" else torch.bfloat16
model = AutoModel.from_pretrained("LiquidAI/d1-2B", trust_remote_code=True, dtype=dtype).to(device)

# Several named questions over one state, answered in one pass
questions = {
    "refund": {"type": "noul", "instructions": "Is the customer asking for a refund?"},  # yes/no: P(yes)
    "team": {"type": "choice", "instructions": "Which team should handle this?",
             "criteria": {"billing": "Charges, refunds, invoices", "shipping": "Delivery and parcels",
                          "technical": "App or site faults"}},
    "topics": {"type": "choice", "multiple": True, "instructions": "Which topics does the message raise?",
               "criteria": {"billing": "Payments and charges", "delivery": "Shipping and parcels",
                            "login": "Signing in to the account"}},
    "urgency": {"type": "score", "instructions": "How urgent is this ticket?", "criteria": ["low", "medium", "high"]},
}
out = model.system_one("I was charged twice and my parcel never arrived. Please refund one charge.", questions)
a = out["answers"]
urgency = a["urgency"]["legend"][str(int(a["urgency"]["score"]))]
print(round(a["refund"]["noul"], 2), a["team"]["choice"], a["topics"]["choices"], urgency)
# 1.0 billing ['billing', 'delivery'] medium

For brevity, we only include the example for d1-2B. See the d1-omni-2B model card for audio clips and spoken questions.

Fine-tune LFM3 for your task

LFM3 is built to be specialized. Frontier models are powerful generalists, but they are not necessarily experts in your use case. LFM3 packs extra capacity into a small, fast model, so a short fine-tune can turn it into a reliable expert on your task, with your data, terminology, and tools. Because it is small, you can deploy the fine-tuned model where your application runs, from devices to private infrastructure to the cloud.

Every model can be fine-tuned on a single GPU, and these notebooks walk you through a complete task for the text, vision, audio, and omni models, from data preparation to evaluation.

ModelMethodTaskNotebook
LFM3-1.7BSFTExtract structured JSON from messy documentsOpen in Colab
LFM3-1.7BDPOAnswer from retrieved documents, or declineOpen in Colab
LFM3-1.7BGRPOCall the right tools in a 108-tool phone appOpen in Colab
LFM3-1.7BCPTLearn a new language (Turkish) from raw textOpen in Colab
LFM3-VL-2BSFTRead receipt photos into JSONOpen in Colab
LFM3-VL-2BGRPOTranscribe images of equations to LaTeXOpen in Colab
LFM3-Audio-2BSFTMap spoken smart-home commands to function callsOpen in Colab
LFM3-Audio-2BSFTTeach the model a new voiceOpen in Colab
LFM3-Omni-2BSFTMap spoken smart-home commands to function callsOpen in Colab
LFM3-Omni-2BSFTAnswer spoken questions about medical imagesOpen in Colab

Example: teaching LFM3 to act

We adapt LFM3-VL-2B into three complementary robotics models for orchestration, navigation, and manipulation. The orchestrator operates a robot arm through tool calls: it grounds objects by pointing, measures them with depth tools, invokes motion planners, and checks outcomes in subsequent camera images. The navigator follows route descriptions using recent RGB observations, predicting spatial targets and a waypoint trajectory in just five tokens. The manipulation VLA maps images, language, and robot state to eight-step chunks of continuous actions in a single forward pass. Jointly trained across 15 embodiments, the VLA achieves 96.2% average success across the four LIBERO suites and 45.7% on RoboCasa-GR1 tabletop tasks, generating action chunks in under 50 ms on a Jetson AGX Orin with TensorRT FP16. These results highlight LFM3-VL-2B as a compact foundation for robotics, spanning high-level planning to low-level control with real-time action generation on embedded hardware.

Watch LFM3-VL-2B handle perception, navigation, and manipulation in this demo video.

Get Started with LFM3

All LFM3 models are open-weight and available on Hugging Face today:

  • Download: the LFM3 collection on Hugging Face, including LFM3-1.7B-Base for your own post-training.
  • Fine-tune: adapt LFM3 to your task with our fine-tuning notebooks.
  • Use in your harness: follow our guide on how to run a local agent, like OpenClaw, Hermes Agent, and Pi.

We can't wait to see what you build.

entries.title: Can we trust LLMs to judge whether a research idea is novel?
entries.content:
allenai/novelty-judge-bench

Viewer • Updated • 3.68k • 238 • 4

Can we trust LLMs to judge whether a research idea is novel?

Enterprise Article

Today we’re releasing Old Ideas, Novel Problems, a new study of how reliably large language models can evaluate the novelty of scientific research ideas. Alongside the paper, we’re publishing a benchmark, data, and code for testing novelty judges, plus an automated pipeline researchers can use to build new evaluation sets.

At Ai2, we’ve been developing AI systems that support different parts of scientific discovery. DataVoyager helps researchers explore and analyze structured data, AutoDiscovery generates and tests hypotheses, and Theorizer synthesizes evidence across large bodies of literature into candidate scientific theories. Together with Asta, these projects point toward systems that can help researchers move from understanding prior work to proposing, testing, and refining new ideas.

But generating research ideas is only part of the challenge of automating scientific discovery. Those ideas also need to contribute something genuinely new, which means these systems need a way to distinguish a novel direction from one that mostly repackages existing work.

That judgment is often handed to another LLM—what we call a novelty judge. Novelty judges assess whether a research idea is new relative to prior work, either on its own or in comparison with another idea. There’s no standard way to build one; research teams choose a model, prompt, evaluation format, reasoning budget, and sometimes a literature-retrieval system. Those choices can materially affect the verdict. Yet these judges are often validated only on human-written papers rather than the AI-generated ideas they are actually meant to evaluate.

Our new benchmark results suggest novelty evaluation itself is far from reliable. Across six LLM judges – GPT-5.1, GPT-5.2, GPT-5.4, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Claude Opus 4.5, and Claude Opus 4.6 – seemingly small changes to the evaluation setup produce dramatically different judgments of the same ideas. In one experiment, changing just a few words in a prompt shifts a model’s accuracy in identifying which of two ideas is more novel by more than 50 percentage points. Retrieval and additional reasoning do not consistently improve judgments, and two purpose-built novelty evaluation systems perform worse than a simple prompted Claude Opus 4.6 baseline.

If AI is going to play a larger role in scientific discovery, we need more dependable ways to tell whether it is actually proposing something new. Our work provides tools for studying that problem, while showing how much remains unresolved.

Building a benchmark for novelty judges

To test how reliably novelty judges can distinguish more novel research ideas from less novel ones, we first needed examples where there was strong evidence about the originality of the underlying scientific contribution.

So we built an automated pipeline around ICLR 2026 peer reviews. Rather than treating paper acceptance as a proxy for novelty, we mined the reviews themselves for passages where reviewers explicitly discussed a contribution’s originality. That distinction is key; a paper can be accepted without being particularly novel as long as it is strong enough in other aspects. Likewise, a rejected paper with an original contribution can have other weaknesses.

We created a high-novelty pool of 154 human-authored research ideas by selecting accepted papers in the top-rated 10% of their ICLR research area whose reviewers positively identified novelty and where no reviewer disputed it. We applied the reverse criteria to build a lower-novelty pool: 145 ideas from rejected papers in the bottom 10% whose reviewers raised originality concerns without any reviewer positively identifying novelty. In a separate check of the review-mining process, an annotator agreed with the extracted novelty-signal polarity in 47 of 50 cases; none of the disagreements would have changed whether a reviewer was counted as praising or disputing the paper’s novelty.

Together, these two pools form our first evaluation setting, Human-Only, which tests whether novelty judges can tell apart human-authored ideas with strong evidence of higher or lower novelty. But in practice, novelty judges are increasingly being used to evaluate AI-generated ideas. So we created a second setting, Human+Generated.

For this pool, we paired the same 154 validated human ideas with 154 ideas produced by a simple LLM generator. We assumed the generated ideas were less novel than their human-authored counterparts; these are weak labels, not verified judgments for every idea. The generator received only a research area and an instruction to propose a novel idea, with no literature search, tools, iteration, or feedback. This gave us a conservative comparison between ideas from a basic generator and contributions from top-10% ICLR papers whose reviewers had explicitly endorsed their originality.

As additional checks, an expert independently reviewed 30 Human+Generated pairs, heavily weighted toward cases our strongest judge got wrong, and we rewrote the human- and AI-generated ideas into a common structure to test whether judges were simply reacting to differences in writing style. The expert preferred the human idea in all 30 pairs and judged none of the generated ideas novel.

Importantly, many of our core findings don’t depend on the labels at all. If two reasonable evaluation setups give opposite answers for the same pair of ideas, that disagreement itself reveals instability.

Small changes can produce very different verdicts

Using our collections of human-authored and AI-generated research ideas, we tested how well six LLM judges – GPT-5.1, GPT-5.2, GPT-5.4, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Claude Opus 4.5, and Claude Opus 4.6 – could evaluate novelty through both pointwise (i.e., absolute novelty ratings) and pairwise (i.e., comparing two ideas to find the most novel) comparisons. We varied one factor at a time: the prompt, reasoning budget, whether the judge could see related papers, how the ideas were formatted, how many judgments were combined into a final verdict, and – for AI-generated ideas – which model generated them.

The largest shifts in performance came from how we prompted the model to judge novelty.

For example, we showed GPT-5.4 the same Human+Generated pairs – each containing one validated human-authored idea and one AI-generated idea – with two prompts. One prompt told the model that reviewers had found exactly one idea in each pair to be novel and asked it to identify which one; the other simply asked which idea was novel. When we switched to the simpler prompt, accuracy dropped from 93.5% to 40.9% – below chance – and the model changed its verdict on more than half of the same pairs.

By contrast, the same prompt change shifted accuracy by only about seven percentage points on the Human-Only dataset, which pairs human-authored ideas with stronger and weaker evidence of novelty. That suggests a novelty judge can appear relatively stable on human-authored research but behave very differently on AI-generated ideas.

That said, human-authored ideas weren’t immune. We saw substantial shifts on the Human-Only dataset as well; the same change moved Claude Opus 4.6 accuracy by 21 points. The shifts were just less severe than on the AI-generated ideas.

There was also no universally better prompt. For example, when judging ideas individually, dropping an instruction that warned judges not to treat trivial or incremental contributions as novel improved accuracy for some judges while reducing it for others. A prompt that works well for one model may not transfer to another, in other words.

We also tested a common use of novelty judges: comparing ideas from two AI generators. We paired ideas from Claude Opus 4.5 with Claude Sonnet 4.5, and GPT-5.4 with GPT-5.1. Across the tested prompt changes, roughly a quarter to a third of verdicts changed on average across six judges. This disagreement can be measured without assuming which generator produces more novel ideas, showing how the choice of judge prompt can affect comparisons between ideation systems.

More search and reasoning didn’t necessarily produce better novelty judgments. We gave GPT-5.6 Sol an extra-high reasoning budget and live, iterative search restricted to arXiv, then compared it with standard-retrieval judges that each saw five pre-retrieved abstracts. (All judges in this comparison ran once per idea on Human+Generated.) The agentic judge scored 0.78 macro-F1 – 11 points behind Claude Opus 4.6 at 0.89, and in roughly the same range as simpler Claude Opus 4.5 and GPT-5.4 setups – while costing roughly 10× more per decision at current API prices. (In this context, macro-F1 measures how well a judge identifies novel and non-novel ideas; higher is better.)

Purpose-built evaluators weren’t more accurate either, despite costing substantially more. On the Human+Generated set, a simple Claude Opus 4.6 prompt using low reasoning and majority voting across three calls achieved 0.854 macro-F1 at a total evaluation cost of $2.59. By comparison, Idea Novelty Checker, a literature-grounded retrieval and reranking pipeline, scored 0.642 at $30.66, while Sakana AI’s AI Scientist, whose novelty evaluator iteratively searches Semantic Scholar, scored 0.772 at $82.05. (Both dedicated evaluators used Claude Opus 4.6, with one call per decision.)

In other words, the simple prompted baseline was both more accurate and considerably cheaper than either purpose-built system.

Taken together, these results suggest that novelty evaluation is particularly brittle on the AI-generated ideas these systems are increasingly being asked to judge.

Toward more reliable evaluation of novel research

Our results suggest that LLM-based novelty evaluation remains a major open problem. Judges that appear reliable on human-authored research may behave differently on AI-generated ideas; prompts that help one model can hurt another; and more search or compute does not necessarily produce more consistent judgments.

Future work should test judges on the kinds of ideas they will actually evaluate, measure sensitivity across prompts and models, improve how prior literature is incorporated, and build benchmarks that can evolve as the scientific literature grows and AI systems improve. Our benchmark and reusable data pipeline are a starting point—researchers can apply them to new peer reviews, other scientific communities, and future generations of novelty judges.

Automated ideation depends on more than generating plausible research directions; we also need ways to tell when those ideas are genuinely new. By making the weaknesses of current novelty judges easier to measure, we hope this release helps researchers build more robust ways to evaluate AI-generated research ideas.

entries.title: Does Your Model Run on AWS Trainium? Look It Up
entries.content:
aws-neuron/torch-neuronx-model-support

Updated • 2.35k • 1

Does Your Model Run on AWS Trainium? Look It Up

Update on GitHub

In a previous post, we introduced TorchNeuron, the native PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium (the 

torch-neuronx
package). With it, Transformers runs its own modeling code on Trainium, as it does on any other device, so any Transformers model on the Hub may run. Which ones actually do?

The torch-neuronx model support Space answers that question for the most popular models on the Hub. It tells you whether a model runs unmodified on Trainium, and gives you the script to run it yourself.

Look up a model

The Space opens on the Selected view: our own selection of models picked among the top models on the Hub by downloads and by trending score. Each row gives the result, the number of Trainium cores the model is sharded over, the wall time of the run (compilation included) and the peak device memory.

To look up a given model, switch to the Trending or Downloads view and type part of its name. These views follow the Hub's own rankings, one task at a time, whether a model was tested or not. When a model was left out on purpose, the Space tells you why (most of the time it was not prioritized, sometimes it is truly incompatible). You can also pick the versions of the Neuron compiler (

neuronx-cc
) and of Transformers to look at.

At the time of writing, only Transformers models are tested, and our selection is limited to 

text-generation
and 
image-text-to-text
models. We plan to expand to diffusers, sentence transformers, and other transformers tasks.

Run it yourself

Select a model to see how to run it. The Space lists the Neuron stack the model was tested on, the packages to install on top of it, and the 

run.py
script that ran. The script follows the recipe of the TorchNeuron announcement: it loads the model with 
from_pretrained
, sharded when it needs to be, then generates with a static cache and 
torch.compile(backend="neuron")
.

On a Trainium2 (

trn2
) instance with that stack, for example in the AWS Neuron Deep Learning Container, install the packages, then run:
python3 run.py

No need for 

torchrun
: the script launches its own 
torch.distributed
ranks when the model is sharded.

A first run starts by compiling the model's graphs. To skip that step, copy the graphs the same compiler built during the test, from the public NEFF cache bucket. The Space gives you the command, with the right compiler version:

hf buckets sync hf://buckets/aws-neuron/torch-neuronx-neff-cache/neuronxcc- /tmp/neff_cache

What "runs" means

Each test loads the model on a 

trn2
instance, sharded over the smallest number of Trainium cores that can hold its weights. Most models are sharded with tensor parallelism. Mixture-of-experts models without a tensor-parallel plan use expert parallelism only. The test then generates 32 tokens and checks them. On a single core, the tokens are compared with those of a CPU run of the same checkpoint. When the model is sharded, a small judge model checks that the text is fluent English.

At the time of writing, only models that fit on 4 Trainium2 devices are tested, which means 16 cores at most. A 

PASS
says nothing about throughput, or about longer generations.

The results are a dataset

Everything the Space shows comes from the public 

aws-neuron/torch-neuronx-model-support
dataset, with one Parquet file per pair of 

neuronx-cc
and library versions.

Each row holds a model's result, the error when it failed, the versions of the whole stack and the 

run.py
that ran. You can query it directly:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_parquet("hf://datasets/aws-neuron/torch-neuronx-model-support/data")
df[df.model_id == "Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B"][["neuronx_cc", "library", "library_version", "neuron_cores", "result"]]

The dataset card gives the exact meaning of each result.

Next time you wonder whether a model runs on Trainium, look it up.

entries.title: Turning Database Grading into RL Rewards: Post-Training Agents with ThinkingBox
entries.content:
One Success Isn't Reliability: Thinkingbox, a Sandbox and Benchmark for Agents in Stateful Business Workflows

Paper • 2608.19741 • Published • 13

Turning Database Grading into RL Rewards: Post-Training Agents with ThinkingBox

Enterprise Article

This is the follow up to our first blog post, The Agent Said It Was Done. The Database Disagreed. ThinkingBox-Training is now available on GitHub.

We built ThinkingBox to evaluate an agent's work by comparing the final database state with the expected outcome. We then used the same kind of executable signal as a reward on training tasks outside ThinkingBox-Bench. For Qwen3.8-27B, average success rose from 51.70% to 60.78%, while tasks completed correctly on all twenty attempts rose from 38 to 107 with 50 GRPO steps.

Figure 1. ThinkingBox turns executable checks of terminal database state into rewards for post-training agents on tasks outside ThinkingBox-Bench.

This is a joint blog by Microsoft and Hugging Face, special thanks to Mirco Milletari and Xiang Jiang from Microsoft, Sergio Paniego from Hugging Face and our former intern Zhuochun Li (University of Pittsburgh) for co-authoring/reviewing efforts.

We built ThinkingBox to catch agents that say they are done when they are not.

Each of its 507 tasks in ThinkingBox-Bench (our benchmark dataset) hands an agent a real backend and a set of tools, lets it work, then checks what really changed in the database. In the first post, we caught a model closing a customer's ticket as resolved while the carrier exception behind it was still open. Nine competent-looking tool calls, one wrong database row.

Then we noticed what we had built. For most tasks, an executable check can return 1 or 0 directly from the final database state. That is not just a grader. This can be a reward function.+

So we constructed a training pool from ThinkingBox-format tasks outside the benchmark and used their executable outcomes as rewards. The catch was choosing which tasks are suitable for agent training: most tasks are either already solved or hopeless for the model in front of you, and both teach it nothing.

Difficulty is policy-relative: a task is hard for the current model only until that model learns it.

We call this offline policy-relative difficulty. We estimated each task's success probability once using the base policy before training and kept the selected training pool fixed throughout the run.

What happened after training

We used offline policy-relative difficulty to build the training pool, then fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B with GRPO for 50 steps. To recap, we evaluate each of the 507 benchmark tasks 20 times. pass@1 measures average success across all 10,140 attempts. pass@20 measures the share of tasks solved at least once. Observed 20/20 measures the share of tasks that pass every recorded attempt.

Table 1. Qwen3.8-27B results before and after 50 steps of GRPO on the offline-selected training pool.

MetricBaseRL fine-tunedChange
Observed 20/2038 (7.50%)→107 (21.10%)+69 tasks
pass@1 (successful attempts)5,242 (51.70%)→6,163 (60.78%)+9.08 pt
pass@20 (tasks solved at least once)453 (89.35%)→446 (87.97%)−7 tasks

Training sharply increased repeatable success, with a small decline in at-least-once coverage. The rest of the post explains how we selected practice tasks, built the reward loop, and measured that tradeoff.

What does that improvement look like on one task? A traveler requests a room downgrade, but company policy requires manager approval first. Before training, the agent changed the booking and issued refunds without approval in 15 of 20 attempts. After RL fine-tuning, it preserved the booking and payment state in all 20.

Figure 2. One corporate hotel-booking task, 20 attempts per model. The base Qwen3.8-27B model changed the booking without required manager approval in 15 attempts. The RL fine-tuned model preserved booking and payment state in all 20; all expected records matched in 19.

Contents

In a hurry? The headline result is above. The implementation is in Run the training stack.

What the benchmark found, in sixty seconds

ThinkingBox-Bench grades agents on the database records they leave behind. Each of its 507 tasks starts a real backend, hands the agent a set of MCP tools and a simulated LLM user with private context, and at the end runs executable checks against the terminal database state. Checks are against the backend record that needs to be correct, not the specific tool calls. This incentivizes the model to discover possibly new solution paths rather than “rediscover” the human-backed solution, that might be suboptimal albeit correct.

In our first post we ran eighteen models through that benchmark twenty times each and reported a gap that headline accuracy hides. Kimi-K3 solved 93.89% of tasks at least once but completed only 68 of 507 tasks (13.41%) on all twenty recorded attempts. Claude Opus 5 inverted it: narrower coverage, far more consistency.

And bigger or better model did not close it. Claude Opus 5.5 scored 0.66 percentage points higher than Claude Opus 5 on pass@1, yet passed exactly the same number of tasks, 241, on all twenty attempts. That gain in headline accuracy bought zero additional dependability.

If you are choosing a model for work that touches production database records, pass@1 should not be read alone. Observed 20/20 shows which tasks succeed on every attempt, which is closer to what production reliability requires.

The executable terminal-state verdict was also the training reward. Before unpacking the training loop, here is what changed on the sealed benchmark.

Results: the dependability column moved

After training Qwen3.8-27B, we evaluated the selected step-50 checkpoint on the 507-task benchmark it had never trained on. The 507 tasks represent an out-of-distribution test set: their domains, databases, and most MCP tools were not encountered during RL training.

Table 2. ThinkingBox-Bench pass@1 (%) by domain, for selected models from our first blog's Table 2 and our fine-tuned model for different domains and overall. Observed 20/20 numbers are over the entire benchmark with 507 tasks. Each model is evaluated on all 507 tasks for 20 repeated trials. Bold marks the column leader; underline marks the runner-up.

ModelRetailAuto insuranceTravelNeobankConsultingOverallObserved 20/20
Claude Opus 5.580.9768.4054.2871.2561.5867.16241 (47.53%)
Claude Opus 580.7165.8049.9570.6266.1966.50241 (47.53%)
GPT-5.476.3362.6568.1265.3454.6065.36128 (25.25%)
GPT-5.6 Sol67.6565.3060.3459.0957.5261.9182 (16.17%)
Qwen3.8-27B RLFT67.9156.4562.6962.4054.5160.78107 (21.10%)
Claude Sonnet 4.672.3554.4058.9456.3954.3159.19102 (20.12%)
GPT-6 Astra71.7346.5555.8760.8756.8358.31231 (45.56%)
Kimi-K382.2450.8061.8341.3551.6357.3768 (13.41%)
Qwen3.8-27B64.0347.8553.4147.8845.6951.7038 (7.50%)

The headline result is the observed-20/20 row in Table 1. A 27B model that initially completed 38 (7.5%) of ThinkingBox-Bench on every attempt now completes 107 (21.1%) on every attempt, almost thrice. For comparison, observed 20/20 for Kimi-K3 is 68, GPT-5.4 with 128, GPT-6 Astra has 231, and Claude Opus 5.5 leads with 241.

Average success and repeatability produce different orderings. In Table 2, we notice that GPT-5.6 Sol scored slightly higher on pass@1 than the RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B (61.91% versus 60.78%) but passed fewer tasks on all 20 recorded attempts: 82 versus 107. Claude Sonnet 4.6 scored lower on pass@1, at 59.19%, yet passed nearly the same number of tasks every time, at 102. Neither metric alone captures the full picture.

The observed pattern is consistent with sharpening: repeatable success rose while at-least-once coverage fell slightly. This is in-line with prior work. One explanation is that probability distribution moved toward trajectories that work repeatedly while some low-probability paths disappeared.

Overall, the model did not become broader. It became more repeatable. The next question is where those gains landed.

Where the gains landed

Figure 3. Domain-level base scores, RLFT scores, and percentage-point changes. Green change cells show gains and red cells show declines; blue shading indicates the score level within each metric.

Pass@1 and observed 20/20 rose in all five domains. Pass@20 was mixed: it increased in neobank and consulting, but declined in retail, travel, and auto insurance. Auto insurance had the largest breadth loss (−7.0 points), while retail had the largest observed-20/20 gain (+24.5 points).

What dependability costs

The first post priced consistency using simple math: divide the estimated cost of the full 20-run campaign by the number of tasks the model passed every single time.

Cost per dependable task = estimated cost of the 507 × 20 campaign ÷ tasks passing 20/20

Applying the same cost math to the fine-tuned checkpoint's measured token usage:

Table 3. Estimated evaluation cost and dependability for base and RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B. Cost per successful attempt divides total estimated campaign cost (507 x 20) by the number of passing attempts.

MeasureBaseRL fine-tunedChange
Campaign cost, 20 runs$925.80→$855.58−7.6%
Cost per successful attempt$0.177→$0.139−21.4%
Tasks passing 20/2038→1072.8× as many
Cost per dependable task$24.36→$8.00−67.2%

At $8.00 per dependable task, the fine-tuned model came close to GPT-5.4 ($6.80), GPT-6 Astra ($7.45), and Claude Opus 5.5 ($7.80) in the companion comparison.

The single-attempt view

Figure 4 prices cost per successful attempt against pass@1.

Figure 4. The golden arrow traces Qwen3.8-27B base pareto cost position to the RLFT (diamond): pass@1 rises from 51.70% to 60.78% while estimated cost per successful attempt falls from $0.177 to $0.139. Ringed circles mark the Pareto cost frontier.

The move places the fine-tuned checkpoint close to GPT-5.6 Sol, although GPT-5.6 Sol remains cheaper and slightly higher on pass@1. Four models priced in our paper fall outside the plotted range.

The dollar values are a comparative serving index, not invoice or cloud bills. Serving the fine-tuned checkpoint would be the same as the base model. The calculation includes model inference cost, and excludes training run and policy-probe cost for curating the training dataset.

These results tell us what moved. The next sections explain the training loop and why selecting the right tasks matters the most.

The training loop

Figure 5. The six stages, now in context: candidate tasks feed in, the first three run once offline, the last three repeat for every group in the training run. The trained checkpoint is evaluated against ThinkingBox-Bench.

Selection runs once, offline, against the base policy model, i.e in this case Qwen3.8 27B; training then uses that fixed pool that has been curated. The dashed amber arrow in Figure 5 marks the path we did not take: re-probing difficulty during the training run.

Every rollout is a complete episode, not a text completion. It gets a fresh backend, an isolated MCP session, and GPT-5 Chat as the simulated user. Most rewards come from deterministic terminal-state checks; a minority of narrow rubric requirements can invoke the configured judge (GPT-5 Chat).

Training and evaluation must interpret Qwen output identically. That includes reasoning extraction, tool calls, argument typing, rendering, and isolated task state. Otherwise the reward measures a different agent from the one evaluated. The shared interpretation code is in 

trainer/core/tb_interpret.py
.

For the reference run, we ran full-parameter RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B on 187 tasks using token-mean GRPO. Each update generated 18 groups of 8 rollouts, or 144 episodes, across 24 H100s. Training ran synchronously with parameter and optimizer offload; AdamW used a 

1e-6
learning rate and zero weight decay. We ran the training for 50 steps.

Zero-variance groups were replaced DAPO-style during training. System errors were handled separately: a backend timeout is not an incorrect agent outcome, so affected groups were refilled rather than scored as failures.

That explains how retained tasks were trained. The remaining question is which tasks entered the training pool.

Offline policy-relative difficulty

Before diving deep into the selection of training tasks, a disclaimer:

No ThinkingBox-Bench task was included in the RL training pool. The benchmark was reserved for evaluation.

ThinkingBox-Bench is out-of-distribution relative to the RL training pool: its domains, databases, policies, and most tools were not encountered during RL training. The two sets still share the ThinkingBox framework, simulated-user machinery, executable terminal-state grading, a few common tools, and a similar task style. These shared elements limit the scope of the transfer claim.

Why selection matters comes down to one arithmetic fact about GRPO. If all eight rollouts fail, the reward vector is 

[0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0]
. If all eight succeed, it is 
[1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1]
. In either case, centering within the group produces no task-reward advantage because no trajectory did better than another.++

A mixed group such as 

[0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1]
supplies the contrast GRPO can learn from. That distinction is expensive for a stateful agent: every rollout provisions an isolated backend, runs a real tool session, and calls a separate model to play the user.

The question that shaped this work was therefore not only which model or optimizer? It was: which candidate tasks should enter the fixed training pool?

We used an offline pass-rate filter on the posterior to select the training pool. It estimates which tasks are likely to produce contrasting terminal rewards under the base policy.

So we probe. Each candidate task is run repeatedly against the base policy model. The plain-language rule is simple: tasks the model always fails are unlikely to teach it yet; tasks it always passes are already learned; tasks it solves sometimes are where outcomes can provide contrast.

Estimating difficulty from limited probes

Each candidate task is run n times, producing k successes. We model its latent success probability with Jeffreys posterior probability:

success probability | k successes in n probes ~ Beta(k + ½, n − k + ½)

Figure 6. Offline policy-relative difficulty is estimated from repeated base-policy probes and used to retain tasks likely to produce contrasting rewards.

We partition the unit interval into five buckets with boundaries at 0.08, 0.40, 0.60, and 0.90, chosen as hyperparameters for these runs. Each task is assigned to the bucket containing the greatest posterior mass:

  • Rarely solved [0, 0.08): drop
  • Difficult [0.08, 0.40): keep
  • Intermediate [0.40, 0.60): keep
  • Frequently solved [0.60, 0.90): keep for full-parameter RLFT
  • Nearly always solved [0.90, 1]: drop

Further details are in Appendix C.4 of our ThinkingBox paper.

One task, end to end

Figure 7. Zooming in, one task through all six stages: GPT-5.4 screening, base-model probes, difficulty classification, a rollout group, terminal-state grading, and a GRPO update.

Figure 7 follows one candidate task that can potentially enter the training pool. For the Qwen3.8 27B full-parameter pool, GPT-5.4 first served as a solvability screen. The base policy then succeeded on few of the probes e.g 3 of 8, producing a Beta(3.5, 5.5) posterior. Its largest mass, 54.0%, fell in the Difficult band.

When sampled for training, the task produced the mixed reward group 

[0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1]
. Successful trajectories therefore received above-mean task advantage and failed trajectories below-mean advantage, giving GRPO contrast to learn from. A different policy model could place the same task in a different difficulty band.

The final Qwen3.8-27B curated training pool contained 187 tasks.

What earns a reward

Nothing about the trajectory. The reward is the task's own executable verdict.

When an episode ends, the sandbox extracts what actually changed in the backend and runs the task's deterministic checks against the terminal state. Any trajectory that produces the correct end state passes. Wrong, missing, or extra side effects fail. The reward is 1 or 0.

In the benchmark, the database grader can be thought of as the “examiner”: it caught agents that reported success and left the wrong record. In training, the same kind of check can be seen as the “teacher” on a different, disjoint set of tasks.

Two reward paths, one binary verdict

  • Executable check (the large majority). When the required outcome is represented in terminal state or side effects, a deterministic test accepts or rejects it; no LLM judge call is needed.
  • Judge-assisted check (a minority). When a narrow requirement cannot be determined cleanly from database state, the configured LLM judge answers a binary rubric question used by the executable test.

Run the training stack

We release the data-selection, rollout, reward, and Verl integration used to train Qwen3.8-27B in microsoft/thinkingbox-training. The repository README is the entry point. The detailed guides are:

  • docs/data-preparation.md
     for task hydration, policy probes, benchmark exclusion, and train/validation splitting;
  • docs/reference-q38-run.md
     for the validated 24-H100 Qwen3.8 configuration;
  • docs/evaluation.md
     for merging a checkpoint and running ThinkingBox-Bench 507 x 20.

Before you start

Tested on Linux and WSL with Python 3.12 and uv. You need NVIDIA GPUs with a compatible CUDA/NCCL stack, a local Qwen3.8-27B checkpoint, and OpenAI-compatible endpoints for the simulated user and judge. The validated reference configuration uses 3 nodes x 8 H100 GPUs; smaller custom configurations depend on model size, context length, and rollout concurrency.

The public sample task list exercises the interface. It is not the private 187-task training pool used for the reported run. Supply an authorized training source that remains disjoint from the public benchmark.

Install

Keep the three repositories side by side:

mkdir -p ~/thinkingbox-workspace
cd ~/thinkingbox-workspace

git clone https://github.com/microsoft/thinkingbox.git
git clone https://github.com/microsoft/thinkingbox-data.git
git clone --branch main https://github.com/microsoft/thinkingbox-training

git -C thinkingbox checkout 892964e7226044e5463ad188da119df838f4bec1
git -C thinkingbox-data checkout thinkingbox-bench-v1.0

Create the validated environment

The released stack targets Linux, Python 3.12, Verl 0.9.0, and the pinned package lock:

cd ~/thinkingbox-workspace/thinkingbox-training

uv venv --python 3.12
source .venv/bin/activate

uv sync --frozen --extra fast --extra tracking --extra eval-proxy
uv pip install -e ../thinkingbox
uv pip install --config-settings editable-mode=compat \
  -e ../thinkingbox-data/servers/thinkingbox_tools
uv pip install --config-settings editable-mode=compat \
  -e ../thinkingbox-data/servers/tb_business_ops_servers_202606

python scripts/prepare_verl.py --dest .deps/verl --install
python scripts/verify_verl_install.py
uv pip check

The final two commands should report a verified patched Verl checkout and no broken requirements. Do not run another automatic package sync afterward: it can replace the patched source installation with the vanilla Verl wheel.

Prepare the training data

Start with the publicly provided samples, or add your own authorized dataset in ThinkingBox format. Then run the repository's preparation script:

cd ~/thinkingbox-workspace/thinkingbox-training
source .venv/bin/activate
python data/prepare_data.py --help

The script aggregates policy probes, applies offline policy-relative difficulty filters and benchmark exclusions, and writes the selected 

train.yaml
and 
test.yaml
files. 
docs/data-preparation.md
 documents the input fields, loader contract, and complete command.

Configure and inspect the launch

Follow 

docs/reference-q38-run.md
to start Typesense and the MCP servers, configure the simulated user and judge, set the model, task-list, checkpoint, and topology variables, and prepare the Ray cluster. Keep credentials in runtime secret injection rather than committed files or shell history.

Before allocating a training job, use the guide's dry-run command:

DRY_RUN=true ./scripts/run_train.sh \
  trainer.total_training_steps=50 \
  trainer.save_freq=5

It must exit zero without starting Ray or allocating GPUs. Read the emitted 

python -m verl.trainer.main_ppo
command and every resolved override before launching the run.

Train

The launcher configures training; it does not provision hosts. On the reference three-node topology, export the same environment on every node, mount 

CHECKPOINT_DIR
at the same absolute path, then start Ray:
# head node
ROLE=head NODE_IP="$HEAD_IP" GPUS_PER_NODE=8 \
  ./scripts/start_ray.sh

# each worker node
ROLE=worker NODE_IP="$WORKER_IP" \
  HEAD_ADDRESS="$HEAD_IP:6379" GPUS_PER_NODE=8 \
  ./scripts/start_ray.sh

After 

ray status
reports all 24 GPUs, launch once from the head node:
export RAY_ADDRESS=auto
export GPUS=0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7

./scripts/run_train.sh \
  trainer.project_name=thinkingbox-training \
  trainer.experiment_name=q38-full-rlft \
  trainer.total_training_steps=50 \
  trainer.save_freq=5

Evaluate the checkpoint through OpenEnv

The first ThinkingBox post covers Typesense, the MCP Session Proxy, and OpenEnv setup. Merge the trained checkpoint following 

docs/evaluation.md
, then serve it with vLLM.

From the OpenEnv repository root, set 

MERGED_MODEL
to the merged model directory and 
THINKINGBOX_DATA
to the pinned benchmark checkout. The historical checkpoint evaluation used this eight-A100 serving configuration:
vllm serve "$MERGED_MODEL" \
  --served-model-name q38-rlft \
  --host 127.0.0.1 \
  --port 8001 \
  --tensor-parallel-size 8 \
  --dtype bfloat16 \
  --max-model-len 262144 \
  --gpu-memory-utilization 0.85 \
  --max-num-seqs 16 \
  --max-num-batched-tokens 8192 \
  --language-model-only \
  --enable-chunked-prefill \
  --enable-prefix-caching \
  --reasoning-parser qwen3 \
  --enable-auto-tool-choice \
  --tool-call-parser qwen3_xml

In a separate terminal, start the OpenEnv compatibility proxy for the Qwen chat template from the ThinkingBox Training checkout. It listens on port 8014 and forwards to vLLM on 8001:

cd ~/thinkingbox-workspace/thinkingbox-training
source .venv/bin/activate
bash scripts/launch_sysmerge.sh

Keep it running during evaluation. From another terminal, check readiness:

curl --fail http://127.0.0.1:8014/readyz

Update the agent entry in the existing 

thinkingbox.yaml
; retain its MCP, simulated-user, and judge configuration:
orchestrator:
  agent_model:
    type: aoai
    endpoint_url: http://127.0.0.1:8014/v1/chat/completions
    deployment: q38-rlft
    credential:
      type: api-key
      api_key: 
    is_reasoning: true
    temperature: 1.0
    top_k: 20
    top_p: 0.95
    max_completion_tokens: 8192
    timeout: 1800

Start OpenEnv as in the first post, with 

OPENENV_TB_CONFIG
pointing to this 
thinkingbox.yaml
and 
OPENENV_TB_DATASET
to 
$THINKINGBOX_DATA
. Once 
/ready
succeeds, run the full protocol of 507 tasks × 20 attempts:
uv run --project envs/thinkingbox_env --frozen \
  thinkingbox-eval \
  --config "$PWD/thinkingbox.yaml" \
  --base-url http://127.0.0.1:8000 \
  --dataset "$THINKINGBOX_DATA" \
  --output q38-rlft-full.jsonl \
  --errors-output q38-rlft-full-errors.jsonl \
  --repeat 20 \
  --coverage-profile full \
  --aggregate-output q38-rlft-full-aggregate.json \
  --message-timeout 1800

The 

full
profile validates all 10,140 expected task/repetition keys before aggregation.

Where this goes next

The useful part of this work is not one Qwen3.8-27B checkpoint. It is the training loop and training data curation that turns executable outcomes into rewards.

If you are training or evaluating an agent that touches real database records:

  • Probe before you train. Take your own agent task set, run the base policy against it n times, and look at the band histogram. In our experience teams often have not inspected this distribution, and it is usually more lopsided than expected.
  • Check your parity. Replay the same recorded model output through the training and evaluation parsers, and verify that both extract identical tool names and arguments. Otherwise, training may reward behavior that evaluation interprets differently.
  • Report both coverage and repeatability. State how many tasks pass at least once in k attempts and how many pass all k. A model that occasionally finds a solution is not necessarily one that repeats it consistently.

Further details can be found in the following links:
